title: Maps, Sets, objects & arrays: choosing the collection
objectives: Choose a `Set` or `Map` over `includes`/`find` inside a loop, and explain why a scan per item is n × m work
Predict key behaviour: object keys become strings and integer-like keys sort first; `Map` keys keep their type and compare by identity
Spot plain-object dictionary traps — inherited keys like `"constructor"`, a `Map` serialising to `{}` — and fix them
Write the everyday moves: dedupe with `new Set`, index with `new Map(list.map(…))`, count, convert, and group with `Object.groupBy`/`Map.groupBy` (ES2024)

questions.prompt: For each of 10,000 incoming events you check whether `event.userId` is one of 5,000 blocked ids. What should `blocked` be?

options.text: A `Set` built once from the ids, checked with `blocked.has(event.userId)`
The array, checked with `includes` — it runs in native code, so it's effectively constant-time
The array sorted ascending, so `includes` can binary-search it
The array, checked with `find` — it stops at the first match, so it's fast

questions.explanation: `Set.has` doesn't scan: the spec requires sublinear access, and MDN notes it is on average faster than `includes` on an array of the same size. `includes` checks elements one by one however fast each check is — native code makes each comparison cheap, not the count smaller. It also has no idea the array is sorted, so sorting buys nothing. And `find` stops early only on a *hit*: most events aren't blocked, so most checks are misses that walk all 5,000 ids.

questions.prompt: A signup form checks once per submit that the chosen country code is in a 250-item array. A reviewer asks you to turn the array into a `Set`. Is it worth it?

options.text: No — one `includes` per submit is a single short scan; the cost shows up only when the scan runs inside a loop
Yes — `includes` is always the wrong choice for membership
Yes — building the `Set` is free, so there is no downside
No — a `Set` is slower than an array until it holds about a million items

questions.explanation: The problem is n × m work: a scan inside a loop over another list. One check of 250 items per submit is nothing. Building a `Set` is itself one pass over the array, so it pays off only when you look things up repeatedly. There is no fixed size where `Set` becomes faster — what matters is how many lookups you do against it.

questions.prompt: In plain JavaScript, users are indexed by numeric id in a plain object (`byId[user.id] = user`). Then `for (const id in byId) if (id === selectedId) …` never matches, though `selectedId` is `7` and user 7 is there. Why?

options.text: Object keys are strings: `id` is `"7"`, and `"7" === 7` is false
`for…in` skips numeric keys
`for…in` iterates the values, so `id` is the user object
Integer keys are stored in a hidden array, so `for…in` can't see them

questions.explanation: An object's keys can only be strings or symbols, so `byId[7]` stores under `"7"`, and `for…in`, `Object.keys` and `Object.entries` all hand it back as a string. `for…in` does visit integer-like keys — first, in ascending order — and it yields keys, not values (`for…of` is the one that yields values, and plain objects aren't iterable with it). Fix: a `Map<number, User>`, or compare `Number(id)`. (In TypeScript the comparison doesn't compile: `string` and `number` have no overlap.)

questions.prompt: `cache.set({ page: 1 }, rows)`, and later `cache.get({ page: 1 })`, where `cache` is a `Map`. What does the `get` return, and why?

options.text: `undefined` — object keys match by identity, and this is a different object
`rows` — the keys have the same contents
`undefined` — a `Map` only accepts primitive keys, so the object key was ignored
It throws a `TypeError` for an object key

questions.explanation: `Map` keys can be any value, objects included, compared with SameValueZero — which for objects means the *same object*. Two literals with equal contents are two objects, so the lookup misses. The "only primitive keys" option has the right result for the wrong reason: the object key was stored fine (`cache.get(sameObject)` would work). For content-based keys, key by a string such as `` `page:${n}` `` or by an id.

questions.prompt: `fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ totals }) })`, where `totals` is a `Map` with two entries. What does the server receive?

options.text: `{"totals":{}}`
Nothing: `JSON.stringify` throws on a `Map`

questions.explanation: `JSON.stringify` visits only own enumerable properties, and a `Map` keeps its entries elsewhere, so it becomes `{}` — silently, with no error (a `Set` does the same). Convert before sending: `[...totals]` for pairs (keys keep their type) or `Object.fromEntries(totals)` for an object (keys become strings), and rebuild with `new Map(…)` on the way back.

questions.prompt: A word counter does `counts[w] = (counts[w] || 0) + 1` on `const counts = {}`. For the word `"constructor"` it stores `"function Object() { [native code] }1"`. Which change fixes it for **every** possible word?

options.text: Count in a `Map`: `counts.set(w, (counts.get(w) ?? 0) + 1)`
Replace `|| 0` with `?? 0`
Write `w in counts ? counts[w] + 1 : 1`
Write `Object.hasOwn(counts, w) ? counts[w] + 1 : 1`, keeping the `{}`

questions.explanation: `{}` inherits `constructor`, `toString` and more from `Object.prototype`, so `counts["constructor"]` starts out as a function. `?? 0` doesn't help (a function isn't nullish), and `in` also sees inherited keys. `Object.hasOwn` fixes `"constructor"` but not `"__proto__"`: assigning `counts["__proto__"] = 1` hits the prototype setter and is silently dropped. A `Map` has no inherited keys at all (so does `Object.create(null)`, which is what `Object.groupBy` returns).

questions.prompt: You want orders grouped by their `customer` **object** (not its id). Which call, and why?

options.text: `Map.groupBy(orders, (o) => o.customer)` — a `Map` keeps object keys as objects
`Object.groupBy(orders, (o) => o.customer)` — it compares keys with SameValueZero, like `Map`
Either: `Object.groupBy` is shorthand for `Map.groupBy` plus `Object.fromEntries`
Neither: both throw when the callback returns an object

questions.explanation: `Object.groupBy` (ES2024) builds an object, so every key is converted to a string — and every customer object becomes `"[object Object]"`, putting all orders in one group. `Map.groupBy` keeps the key as returned. One catch from MDN: to read a group back you need the *same* customer object, so keep the references (or group by `o.customer.id`).

prompts.prompt: Turn the list of tags into a list with each tag once, keeping first-seen order.
prompts.explanation: A `Set` ignores a value it already holds, and iterates in insertion order — the order each value was *first* added. Spreading it (or `Array.from(set)`) turns it back into an array.

prompts.prompt: Index customers by id once, then look each order's customer up in constant time on average.
prompts.explanation: `new Map(…)` takes `[key, value]` pairs — here `[c.id, c]`. Building it is one pass over `customers`; after that each order costs one `get` instead of a `find` scan. `get` returns `undefined` for a missing key, which is why the `?.` is there.

prompts.prompt: Count how often each word appears, starting from 0 the first time a word is seen.
prompts.explanation: `get` returns `undefined` for an unseen word, so fall back to 0 and add one. `??` (only `null`/`undefined` fall back) states the intent; `||` also works here because a stored count is never 0. Unlike a plain object, the `Map` has no inherited `"constructor"` entry to trip over.

prompts.prompt: Save `customersById`, a `Map<number, Customer>`, to `localStorage` and load it back with numeric keys intact.
prompts.explanation: Stringifying the `Map` itself writes `{}`. An array of `[key, value]` pairs survives JSON, and `new Map(pairs)` rebuilds it. Pairs also keep `7` a number; going through `Object.fromEntries` would bring it back as the string `"7"`, and `restored.get(7)` would miss.

prompts.prompt: Group orders by the `customer` object itself, keeping object keys as objects (ES2024).
prompts.explanation: `Map.groupBy` returns a `Map` whose keys are whatever the callback returned. `Object.groupBy` would stringify every customer object to `"[object Object]"` and lump all orders into one group. Use `Object.groupBy` when the keys are naturally strings, like a status.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: Two surprises. The numeric keys come back as strings, because object keys are strings. And they come first, in ascending numeric order — integer-like keys always precede other string keys, which keep insertion order. That's why an object keyed by id iterates in id order, not the order you inserted. A `Map` iterates in insertion order, whatever the keys.

snippets.question: What is logged?
acceptable: 2, then the Object function's source text with 1 appended
snippets.explanation: `counts.to` is 2 as expected. But `counts["constructor"]` is not missing on a fresh `{}` — it is the inherited `Object` function. A function is truthy, so `|| 0` keeps it, and function + 1 converts the function to its source text and concatenates `"1"`. Any word that names an `Object.prototype` member (`toString`, `valueOf`, `hasOwnProperty`, …) does the same. Count in a `Map`.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `1` and `"1"` are different `Map` keys (an object would have merged them into `"1"`), so the size is 3. `get(NaN)` finds its entry even though `NaN !== NaN`, because `Map` uses SameValueZero, which treats `NaN` as equal to itself. `get([1])` misses: the array literal is a new object, and object keys match by identity. (`set` returns the map, which is why the calls chain.)
